why: r77 promised to run the same configuration three times and report the spread before quoting any number again. Every number in r73-r77 was a single seed.

the_implication_for_every_number_quoted_.conclusion: 'text nodes moved it by two tasks' and 'the gate moved it by one' are both INSIDE the noise floor. Neither claim survives three runs.

the_implication_for_the_published_compar.but: the systems near 15-20% are within one or two seeds of each other, and agent benchmarks in this range routinely report single-seed numbers. The ranking at the bottom of the table is not resolvable at n=1.

one_flip_explained.variance_verdict: 0/6 failures reproduced in isolation. The full runner flips on this task; the isolated path is 6/6.
one_flip_explained.so: at least part of the measured variance is a BUG in my sequencer, not irreducible variance. The 8 unstable tasks are not all coin flips; some are a code path I have not isolated.

what_is_now_law: no number from this benchmark is quoted without at least three runs and a spread. Single-seed scores at this level of accuracy are not measurements, they are anecdotes.
next: find the sequencer bug behind the unstable tasks
then, and only then, quote a number with its spread

refusal_vs_acting.if_those_had_refused: score recovers 14.20 points, win count unchanged
refusal_vs_acting.conclusion: refusing does NOT win tasks. It raises the score and removes wrong-but-confident actions. The benchmark publishes only the win count, so the safety property that the gate provides is INVISIBLE to the metric everyone quotes. That is a property of the benchmark, not of the gate.
refusal_vs_acting.note: no honest probability of success is available for those 15 actions, so no refusal policy was run; the 14.20 is an upper bound on what refusing every one of them would recover
